chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Mechanics of Competitive Devaluation

lessons.title: How Central Banks Devalue: Rate Cuts, Intervention, and Jawboning

body.text: A central bank has exactly four ways to push its own currency down: cut interest rates, sell it directly in the market, talk it down without spending a rupee or a franc, or reset the official rate by decree. Every episode in this course, from 1934 to 2015, is one of these four tools, or some combination of them.

children.text: Four Tools, One Goal

Chapter 1 established what a competitive devaluation is and traced two very different historical episodes. This lesson opens up the actual toolkit: the specific levers a central bank pulls when it wants a weaker currency, ranked roughly from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and immediate.
Tool 1: Interest Rate Cuts

markDefs.definition: A theory in international finance stating that the interest rate differential between two currencies should roughly equal the expected rate of currency depreciation, so that expected returns are equalised across currencies with no riskless arbitrage.

children.text: Cutting rates is the cheapest lever available and usually the first one pulled. Lower yields make a currency less attractive to hold, prompting capital to look elsewhere for return, which weakens the currency. The theoretical anchor here is
uncovered interest rate parity
, which says a currency with a higher interest rate should be expected to depreciate against a lower-yielding one by roughly the size of the rate gap, over the relevant horizon.

body.caption: Uncovered interest rate parity: the higher-yielding currency is expected to depreciate by roughly the rate differential

body.title: Apply Interest Rate Parity
body.prompt: Currency A carries a 6% interest rate, Currency B carries 2%, a differential of 4 percentage points. Under uncovered interest rate parity, by roughly what percentage should Currency A be expected to depreciate against Currency B over the next year for expected returns to equalise?
body.explanation: Uncovered interest rate parity predicts Currency A depreciates by roughly the 4 percentage point rate gap, so a foreign investor holding either currency ends up with roughly the same expected return. In practice this often fails to hold over short horizons, a well documented anomaly known as the forward premium puzzle, which is exactly why carry trades of the kind covered in Chapter 1 have historically been profitable rather than arbitraged away.

body.text: If uncovered interest rate parity held perfectly and immediately, the carry trade covered in Chapter 1 would not exist, because any extra yield from holding a higher-rate currency would be exactly offset by its expected depreciation. The forward premium puzzle, the empirical finding that higher-yielding currencies often hold steady or even strengthen in the short run instead of depreciating on schedule, is precisely why that trade has been profitable often enough to keep attracting capital into the rate-cutting country's target markets.

children.text: When ordinary rate cuts run out of room at or near zero, central banks have occasionally gone further, into negative territory: the European Central Bank from 2014, the Swiss National Bank from December 2014, and the Bank of Japan from 2016 all charged commercial banks to park reserves with them, specifically to push money out of the currency and weaken it further.
Tool 2: Direct Market Intervention

markDefs.definition: Central bank buying or selling of its own currency in the open market, sold to push it weaker or bought to support it. Sterilised intervention offsets the resulting change in domestic money supply through separate bond operations; unsterilised intervention lets it feed through.

children.text: Rate cuts work slowly, and sometimes a central bank wants to cap a currency's strength immediately. That is
direct market intervention
: selling the domestic currency and buying foreign currency (usually dollars or euros) outright, in whatever size is needed to move the price.

The clearest example of this tool used at full force by a developed-market central bank is the Swiss National Bank between 2011 and 2015. As the eurozone debt crisis pushed investors toward the franc as a safe haven, the SNB announced on 6 September 2011 that it would defend a floor of 1.20 francs per euro with, in its own words, unlimited quantities of foreign currency purchases. For over three years it did exactly that, printing francs to buy euros whenever the exchange rate threatened to break below 1.20, effectively holding the franc artificially weaker than the market alone would have made it.

body.label: SNB's franc floor
body.value: 1.20 francs per euro, defended Sept 2011 to Jan 2015
body.context: Defended with unlimited euro purchases, a rare case of a developed-market central bank openly committing to hold its currency at a specific, weaker-than-market level

body.text: On 15 January 2015, the SNB abruptly abandoned the floor, judging the cost of unlimited intervention unsustainable as the ECB prepared its own quantitative easing programme. The franc surged against the euro within minutes, at the most extreme intraday moves briefly gaining roughly 30% before settling into a smaller but still large appreciation by the end of the day, an event still referred to in currency markets as the Swiss franc shock. The lesson is not subtle: direct intervention can hold a level for years, but the moment a central bank stops defending it, the market repricing can be violent and immediate.

children.text: Tool 3: Jawboning

markDefs.definition: A central bank or finance ministry official publicly signalling displeasure with a currency's level or direction, attempting to move the market through words and implied future action alone, without actually intervening.

children.text: The cheapest tool of all costs nothing but a press statement.
Jawboning

is a finance ministry or central bank official warning that a currency's move is excessive or unwelcome, hoping traders price in the risk of future intervention and adjust their positions pre-emptively. Japan's Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Japan have used this repeatedly over the years, issuing verbal warnings about excessive yen strength well before, and sometimes instead of, actually entering the market.

Jawboning is cheap exactly because it works only as long as it is credible. A central bank that talks tough repeatedly without ever following through eventually gets ignored by the market, at which point it has to either escalate to real intervention or accept it has lost this tool's effectiveness for a while.
Tool 4: Administrative Devaluation

The bluntest tool is simply resetting the official rate by decree, the mechanism behind every episode already covered in this course: the US raising the official gold price to $35 an ounce in 1934, China cutting the yuan's daily reference rate in August 2015, and India's own two-step devaluation in July 1991. This tool only exists where a central bank has an official rate or reference peg to reset in the first place, which is precisely why it has become rarer as more major currencies have moved to floating, managed regimes.

Expensive to sustain, and abrupt exit risk

body.title: Quick Check: Which Tool Is This?
body.question: A central bank governor tells reporters the currency's recent strength is 'unwarranted and not justified by economic fundamentals,' without any actual purchase or sale of currency that week. Which tool is this?
body.explanation: This is jawboning: an attempt to move market expectations through words alone. It costs nothing directly, but it only stays effective if the market believes real intervention could follow if the warnings are ignored.

children.text: When Central Banks Coordinate Instead of Compete: Japan, March 2011

Not every episode of central banks moving a currency is competitive. After the devastating Tohoku earthquake and tsunami on 11 March 2011, the yen spiked to a record high near ¥76 to the dollar within days, driven by expectations that Japanese insurers and companies would repatriate overseas assets to fund reconstruction and claims. A stronger yen was the last thing Japan's earthquake-hit exporters needed.

events.title: Tohoku earthquake and tsunami
events.description: A magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami devastate Japan's northeast coast, triggering fears of forced yen repatriation by Japanese firms and insurers.

events.title: Yen hits a record high
events.description: The yen spikes to roughly ¥76 to the dollar, its strongest level on record at the time, adding currency pressure on top of the physical disaster.

events.title: Coordinated G7 intervention
events.description: The G7 central banks intervene jointly to sell yen and weaken it, the first coordinated G7 currency intervention in over a decade, explicitly framed as disaster support rather than a competitive move.

body.text: This is the mirror image of everything else in this lesson. Japan's trading partners did not accuse it of a currency war, they actively helped weaken the yen, because everyone agreed the spike was a disaster-driven distortion rather than Japan chasing a competitive advantage. The tools are identical to a currency war, rate policy, intervention, jawboning, what differs entirely is the motive and whether other countries see themselves as the ones absorbing the cost.

body.title: You Advise a Central Bank Governor
body.scenario: Your currency has strengthened 8% against the dollar over two months, driven by strong capital inflows. Exporters are furious. You have already issued two rounds of verbal warnings about the strength being unjustified, but the currency kept climbing through both. Your reserves are healthy but not unlimited, and your policy rate is already at a level you're reluctant to cut further given a stubborn domestic inflation problem.
body.prompt: Jawboning has failed twice. What do you recommend next, and what is the risk of that recommendation?
body.modelAnswer: With jawboning already discredited by two ignored warnings, the credible next step is either direct intervention or accepting the appreciation. Rate cuts are constrained here by the inflation problem stated in the prompt, so pushing that lever risks a worse domestic outcome than the currency issue itself. Direct intervention (selling the domestic currency, buying dollars) can work immediately, but it needs to be sized credibly: a small, hesitant intervention that fails to move the market is worse than no intervention at all, since it burns reserves and further erodes credibility, as the two failed jawboning rounds already have. If reserves are not deep enough to sustain a serious defence, and the appreciation is being driven by fundamentals (like a strong export sector or high real yields) rather than transient speculation, the harder but more honest recommendation is to accept the move, communicate clearly why, and focus support on affected exporters through other channels instead of a forex fight that is unlikely to be won cheaply.

cards.definition: The theory that the interest rate differential between two currencies should roughly equal the expected rate of depreciation of the higher-yielding one.
The empirical finding that higher-yielding currencies often fail to depreciate as uncovered interest rate parity predicts, helping explain why carry trades are often profitable.
Central bank currency intervention paired with offsetting bond operations, so the domestic money supply effect is neutralised.
Verbal warnings from officials meant to move currency markets without any actual intervention, effective only as long as it is credible.
A one-off, decreed reset of an official exchange rate or reference peg, the bluntest and most visible devaluation tool.

points: Central banks have four tools to weaken a currency: rate cuts, direct market intervention, jawboning, and administrative devaluation, ranging from cheap and slow to blunt and immediate.

Uncovered interest rate parity predicts a higher-yielding currency should depreciate by roughly its rate advantage, but the forward premium puzzle means this often fails to hold in practice, which is exactly why carry trades can be profitable.

The Swiss National Bank's 2011 to 2015 franc floor shows direct intervention can hold a level for years, but abandoning it can trigger a violent, near-instant repricing, as the January 2015 Swiss franc shock demonstrated.
Jawboning is free but fragile: it only works as long as the market believes real action will follow if warnings are ignored.

Not every coordinated currency move is a currency war. The G7's March 2011 intervention to weaken the yen after the Tohoku disaster used the same tools as any currency war episode, but for stabilisation, not competitive advantage.
The next lesson takes this same toolkit and applies it specifically to how the RBI defends the rupee in practice.
